title: What workplace violence training must Washington hospitals and health care settings provide?
description: RCW 49.19: health care workplace violence plans, training within 90 days of hire, 11 required topics, five-year incident records and 2026 investigation rules.
shortAnswer: Chapter 49.19 RCW requires Washington hospitals, home health, hospice and home care agencies, evaluation and treatment facilities, behavioral health programs and ambulatory surgical facilities to keep a workplace violence prevention plan and train applicable employees, volunteers and contracted security staff. Training must occur within 90 days of hire, recur on a schedule set by the plan, and cover up to 11 listed topics. Violent act records are kept for five years.
keyTakeaways: RCW 49.19.030 has required violence prevention training since July 1, 2020, for applicable employees, volunteers and contracted security personnel as determined by the plan.
New employees must be trained within 90 days of their initial hire date, unless they are temporary employees.
Training frequency and method are set by the facility's plan, but content must address the listed topics as appropriate to the setting and the employee's duties.
Since January 1, 2026, every workplace violence incident must be investigated and summaries sent to the committee at least quarterly (twice yearly for certain small and rural hospitals).
The plan must be comprehensively reviewed and updated at least once per calendar year, and failure to comply can be cited under chapter 49.17 RCW.
regulator: Washington State Department of Labor and Industries (L&I)
appliesTo: Home health, hospice and home care agencies under chapter 70.127 RCW, evaluation and treatment facilities, behavioral health programs, and ambulatory surgical facilities
Applicable employees, volunteers and contracted security personnel, as determined by the facility's plan

sections.heading: Which Washington health care settings are covered by RCW 49.19?

blocks.text: Five types of health care setting are covered. RCW 49.19.010 defines a "health care setting" as hospitals under RCW 70.41.020; home health, hospice and home care agencies under chapter 70.127 RCW; evaluation and treatment facilities under RCW 71.05.020; behavioral health programs under RCW 71.24.025; and ambulatory surgical facilities under RCW 70.230.010. The Department of Labor and Industries enforces the chapter.

The legislature's 1999 findings in RCW 49.19.005 state that, based on workers' compensation claims, "health care employees face the highest rate of workplace violence in Washington state." The chapter was substantially amended in 2019, effective January 1, 2020, and again in 2025, with investigation and data summary duties effective January 1, 2026. This page states the position as at November 2026.

Workplace violence is defined broadly: "any physical assault or verbal threat of physical assault against an employee of a health care setting on the property of the health care setting," including assaults or threats involving a firearm or a common object used as a weapon, whether or not anyone is injured.

sections.heading: What does RCW 49.19.030 require for training?

blocks.text: Each covered setting must provide violence prevention training "to all applicable employees, volunteers, and contracted security personnel, as determined by the plan," by July 1, 2020, and on a regular basis after that. Training must occur within 90 days of the employee's initial hiring date, except for temporary employees.

The statute leaves method and frequency to the plan. It lists acceptable formats, including classes with interactive questions and answers, hands-on training, video, brochures, and verbal or written training "determined to be appropriate under the plan." That flexibility makes the plan the controlling document: an inspector will compare what the plan says about frequency and audience with the training records.

blocks.title: Not the same as Washington's general safety orientation
blocks.text: Covered settings must still meet the accident prevention program and safety orientation rules in chapter 296-800 WAC. RCW 49.19 adds a violence-specific plan and training on top. See [Washington accident prevention program training](/regulations/washington-accident-prevention-program-training).

sections.heading: What topics must the training address?

blocks.text: Training must address 11 topics, "as appropriate to the particular setting and to the duties and responsibilities of the particular employee being trained, based upon the hazards identified in the plan." Not every employee needs every topic in depth; the plan's hazard assessment decides. The table below suggests how a hospital might assign them.

blocks.text: Topic (f) explicitly calls for hands-on practice or role play, which an online module alone cannot provide. Topic (h) overlaps with federal restraint and seclusion requirements for hospitals; see [CMS hospital Conditions of Participation training](/regulations/cms-hospital-conditions-of-participation-training).

sections.heading: What must the workplace violence prevention plan contain?

blocks.text: The plan must address security considerations and factors that contribute to or prevent violence, including the facility's physical attributes, staffing and procedures to reduce time spent alone in high-risk areas, job design, first aid and emergency procedures, reporting, "employee education and training requirements and implementation strategy," unit-specific and parking area security risks, and assistance to employees affected by a violent act.

Where a setting has a safety committee under RCW 49.17.050, or a workplace violence committee in which employee-elected members equal or outnumber employer-selected members, that committee develops, implements and monitors the plan. Under the 2025 amendment, the setting or committee must conduct "a comprehensive review and update of the workplace violence prevention plan at least once per calendar year." When the plan's training section changes, the training content should follow.

sections.heading: What records and investigations are required?

blocks.text: Every violent act against an employee, patient or visitor must be recorded and the record kept for at least five years. RCW 49.19.040 lists the minimum fields, including date, time and location, the victim's job title and unit if an employee, who committed the act, a six-level severity scale from threat without contact to loss of limb or death, any weapon used, the number of employees nearby, and actions taken in response.

Since January 1, 2026, RCW 49.19.080 also requires a timely investigation of every incident, assessing details, response and remediation, and, if applicable, actual against planned staffing. The setting must send the committee a de-identified summary with an analysis of systemic causes and recommendations for changing the plan. Summaries are due at least quarterly, or at least twice per year for critical access hospitals, hospitals with fewer than 25 acute care beds in operation, certain sole community hospitals, and a hospital on an island in a Skagit County public hospital district.

These summaries are a direct input to training. If investigations show that most incidents occur during patient transfers or in the emergency department waiting area, the plan and the training should change accordingly. See [how to use training in a CAPA](/guides/how-to-use-training-in-a-capa) and [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

Failure to comply subjects the health care setting to citation under chapter 49.17 RCW, the Washington Industrial Safety and Health Act, according to RCW 49.19.050. For home health, hospice and home care agencies, RCW 49.19.070 directs the department to allow "sufficient flexibility in recognition of the unique circumstances in which these agencies deliver services," since care is delivered in patients' homes rather than in a facility.

RCW 49.19.060 also states that the Departments of Labor and Industries, Social and Health Services, and Health are to collaborate with health care settings on technical assistance and training seminars on plan development.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each of the 11 statutory topics to the plan's hazard assessment by unit and role, so the depth of training follows the risk the plan identifies. When a quarterly investigation summary recommends a plan change, the affected topics and roles are identifiable. See [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: How soon must new hospital staff in Washington receive violence prevention training?
faqs.a: Within 90 days of the employee's initial hiring date, unless the employee is temporary. The plan then sets how often training is repeated, since RCW 49.19.030 requires training on a regular basis as set out in the plan.

faqs.q: Does RCW 49.19 require annual workplace violence training?
faqs.a: The statute does not fix an annual interval for training; it leaves method and frequency to the plan. The plan itself must be comprehensively reviewed and updated at least once per calendar year, which usually prompts a review of training frequency too.

faqs.q: Do volunteers and contract security officers need training?
faqs.a: Yes, where the plan determines they are applicable. RCW 49.19.030 requires training for all applicable employees, volunteers and contracted security personnel, as determined by the plan.

faqs.q: Can the training be delivered by video?
faqs.a: Video is one of the formats the statute lists, along with interactive classes, hands-on training and written materials. However, the topic on strategies to prevent physical harm must include hands-on practice or role play, so a video-only program would not cover every topic.
